
# 3D Cell Detection

## Cellfinder

Cellfinder is the BrainGlobe tool for detecting cell coordinates

## Applications

Goal: find centre coordinates of bright spots (fluorescently labelled cells)

* Viral tracing
* cFos (experimental support)
* Maybe others?

## Why is 3D cell detection hard? {.smaller}

![](img/whole.png){.nostretch fig-align="center" width=62%}

Pure machine-learning based methods are slow on such large data (~100GB per channel)

## `cellfinder` strategy

Best of both worlds

* Select too many possible cells: "candidates"
* Use machine-learning to classify candidates as cell/not cell
    * needs curation and re-training

## `cellfinder` candidate detection

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
A series of image filters on the signal channel only

:::{.incremental}
1. 2D filters
2. 3D filters
3. Structure splitting
:::

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](img/input_closeup.png)
:::
:::

## 2D filter {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[1. Clip to reserve 2 values]{.fragment fragment-index="1"}

[2. Keep tiles with average intensity > avg+2*std(corner tiles)]{.fragment fragment-index="2"}

[3. Enhance peaks]{.fragment fragment-index="3"}

    [a) median filter]{.fragment fragment-index="3"}

    [b) gaussian filter]{.fragment fragment-index="3"}

    [c) laplacian filter]{.fragment fragment-index="3"}

[4. Threshold at plane avg+nds*std]{.fragment fragment-index="4"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.r-stack}
![](img/clipped.png){.fragment fragment-index="1"}

![](img/clipped.png){.fragment fragment-index="2"}

![](img/enhanced.png){.fragment fragment-index="3"}

![](img/filtered_2d.png){.fragment fragment-index="4"}
:::
:::
:::

## 3d filter + structure splitting {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[1. Looks at sphere (ellipsoid) around each pixel]{.fragment fragment-index="1"}
    [a) If sufficient pixels in the ellipsoid are bright, mark as candidate]{.fragment fragment-index="1"}

[2. If needed structure is big, split it.]{.fragment fragment-index="2"}

[3. Compute and return centres of structures]{.fragment fragment-index="3"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.r-stack}

![](img/struct_type_closeup.png){.fragment fragment-index="2"}

![](img/struct_type_split_closeup.png){.fragment fragment-index="3"}
:::
:::
:::

## Curation and retraining

Suggested strategy

* spend hours, not days curating
* iterate fast: curate, retrain, classify and repeat
* curated balanced data (equal number of cells/not cells)

Reminder: only candidate cells will be classified

## Practical notes for users

Similar to other BrainGlobe tools, `cellfinder` has

* `napari` interface (as seen today)
* Python API

and additionally,

* part of a command line interface for detection and classification ("brainmapper")

## Interoperability with OME zarr

The Python API enables interoperability with the wider Python ecosystem.

```{.python}
from cellfinder.core import main as cellfinder_run 

# open your OME Zarr image here

cellfinder_run(...)

```

## Interoperability with other tools

The Python API enables interoperability with the wider Python ecosystem.

```{.python}
from cellfinder.core.detect import main as cellfinder_detect

candidates = cellfinder_detect(...)

classify_candidates_custom(candidates, ...)

```

## Implementation notes

* implemented within the `pytorch` framework
* uses custom multithreading and multiprocessing
    * works particularly well on nvidia GPUs
* highly optimised data loading

Matt Einhorn, Cleland Lab, Cornell

## Performance-related parameters

* defaults chosen sensibly, for typical applications

longer term

## Key take-aways

* `cellfinder` can be used to efficiently find cells in large whole-brain microscopy images
* it uses classical image filtering to find candidates and then classifies them
    * candidates can include many false positives, but _must_ include _all_ true positives
    * usually classification model needs curation and retraining
